tagline: A curving river road beside a reservoir that submerged its predecessor
intro: The Upper Yadkin Way follows NC 268 from US 321 toward W. Kerr Scott Dam and Reservoir. The highway curves northeast from its western end, roughly following the Yadkin River, then runs along the reservoir’s southern shore toward Wilkesboro. This is a rural stretch of a highway connecting northwestern North Carolina’s mountains and foothills.

NC 268 reached Patterson in 1933, extending west through Wilkesboro to US 321. A larger change came in 1962, when the highway was rerouted south of the future reservoir. Most of that former alignment was abandoned and submerged; Old NC 268 remained. The dam was completed that year to control recurring floods.

Begin at US 321 north of Lenoir and follow NC 268 northeast. Fort Defiance lies on the Yadkin, followed along the journey by Ferguson on NC 268. Continue toward the reservoir, where the highway follows the south shore toward Wilkesboro.

moments.title: Fort Defiance
moments.text: Fort Defiance is a plantation house on a site that had already served a military purpose. Troops under Elijah Isaacs built here in the summer of 1776, when the place was known as Fort Isaacs. The later home of Revolutionary War General William Lenoir took shape between 1788 and 1792. Its main block is a two-story frame building measuring 28 by 40 feet; a wing was added in 1823. The property passed to the Caldwell County Historical Society in 1965 and operated as a house museum. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1970.

moments.title: Ferguson
moments.text: Ferguson, on NC 268, has a connection to the folk song “Tom Dooley.” Whippoorwill Academy and Village includes a museum relating to Tom Dula. The community’s historic associations also include the graves of Dula, Laura Foster and Anne Melton, three people involved in the murder case remembered in song.

moments.title: W. Kerr Scott Reservoir
moments.text: W. Kerr Scott Reservoir occupies part of the former highway’s course. In 1962, NC 268 moved south of the future lake, leaving most of its old alignment to be submerged. The dam was completed the same year to control flooding that had repeatedly troubled the area. Named for Governor W. Kerr Scott, who played a key role in the project, the reservoir is managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The artificial lake covers 1,475 acres and has 56 miles of shoreline. NC 268 follows its southern shore. Old NC 268 is the surviving remnant of the former route.
